title: Latency vs Throughput & Tail Latency
intro: System performance is governed by two complementary metrics: Latency (time to complete a unit of work) and Throughput (rate at which work is completed).
objectives: Apply Little's Law ( = \lambda W$) to compute concurrency and queue capacity.
Analyze why arithmetic averages hide tail latency and why P99/P99.9 matter.
Mitigate tail amplification in parallel fan-out microservice architectures.
body:
### Little's Law
Little's Law states that the average number of requests $ in a stable system equals the arrival rate $\lambda$ multiplied by the average latency $:

23L = \lambda 	imes W23

For example, if a service processes 10,000 req/sec ($\lambda$) with an average latency of 50ms (bash.05s$), the concurrent in-flight requests in the system is  = 10,000 	imes 0.05 = 500$ concurrent requests.

### Tail Latency Amplification
In a distributed system, a single user request often fans out to $ backend microservices in parallel. If each service has a 1% chance of experiencing a P99 latency spike (99% fast), the probability that the user request experiences a spike is:

23P(	ext{user hits slow service}) = 1 - (1 - 0.01)^N23

With =20$ services,  - 0.99^{20} pprox 18.2\%$ of user requests suffer tail latency!
keyIdea: Averages lie; tail latency governs user happiness. In parallel fan-out systems, tail latencies compound exponentially.

concepts.title: Hedged Requests
concepts.body: Issuing a duplicate redundant request to a replica after the P95 timeout threshold to race the slower one.

concepts.title: HDR Histograms
concepts.body: High Dynamic Range histograms record latency measurements with microsecond precision across arbitrary orders of magnitude.

examples: Google search issuing duplicate query replicas to eliminate tail latency.
Netflix Hystrix isolating thread pools to prevent tail latency cascades.

quiz.prompt: If a service receives 5,000 RPS and takes 20ms on average to process a request, how many concurrent requests are in flight?
quiz.explanation: By Little's Law: L = 5000 * 0.02 = 100 concurrent requests.
